rd-2026-10-25-medicare-s-new-hospice-cra.title: Medicare's new hospice crackdown mostly flagged hospices serving Black patients, and usually over a single metric
rd-2026-10-25-medicare-s-new-hospice-cra.angle: CMS's Hospice Special Focus Program was built to catch failing hospices. A census of all 7,115 US hospices shows the first 50 it picked served about twice the share of non-White patients (median 35% vs 17%, driven by Black patient share), and the gap held after adjusting for quality. For 48 of the 50, one input drove most of the failing score. That raises the question of whether the algorithm is measuring care or measuring who gets served.
rd-2026-10-25-medicare-s-new-hospice-cra.why_now: Published online 6 days ago, and the program is already paused amid litigation, so there is a live policy fight with a court clock.
rd-2026-10-25-medicare-s-new-hospice-cra.is_it_real: Solid for what it claims. It covers every active hospice in the November 2024 CMS data, so this is a census, not a sample. It is cross-sectional and observational: it shows who was flagged and why, not that the flagged hospices give good care. It is a single snapshot of a program that has since been paused. The pitch agents should confirm the litigation status and what CMS has said since.
rd-2026-10-25-medicare-s-new-hospice-cra.other_peg: The Special Focus Program is paused amid litigation, and CMS's next move on hospice oversight is pending.

studies.journal: The American Journal of Hospice & Palliative Care
studies.headline: The federal program flagging hospices for poor care disproportionately targeted those serving Black patients — and usually based on a single failing metric
studies.caveats: observational design, cross-sectional, single time-point snapshot, program subsequently paused amid litigation

rd-2026-10-25-a-six-week-phone-guided-ex.title: A six-week, phone-guided exercise plan sped recovery from lingering teen concussions in a randomized trial
rd-2026-10-25-a-six-week-phone-guided-ex.angle: Parents still hear 'rest in a dark room' for concussions. In a JAMA Pediatrics randomized trial of 210 kids aged 11 to 18 in four states, graduated aerobic exercise delivered remotely (activity trackers plus weekly video calls) beat stretching for symptom recovery and quality of life at three months. The biggest benefit came when it started within three months of the injury. The service angle is that it needs no clinic visits, which matters for rural families.
rd-2026-10-25-a-six-week-phone-guided-ex.why_now: Online 6 days ago and not covered yet. It's mid fall sports season, when youth football and soccer concussions peak.
rd-2026-10-25-a-six-week-phone-guided-ex.is_it_real: One of the stronger studies today: randomized, controlled, multi-state, 210 participants, in a top pediatrics journal. The control was stretching, not rest, so it shows aerobic exercise beats light activity, not that it beats doing nothing. Benefit was concentrated in kids injured less than three months earlier. The shift away from strict rest is already in concussion guidance, so the news is remote delivery and the effect in prolonged cases, not 'exercise helps' by itself.

studies.headline: A Phone-Based Exercise Program Helps Teens Recover Faster From Prolonged Concussion — No Clinic Visits Required
studies.caveats: narrow age range

rd-2026-10-25-the-hispanic-health-parado.title: The 'Hispanic health paradox' in birth outcomes may come down to how researchers measure education
rd-2026-10-25-the-hispanic-health-parado.angle: For decades, researchers have pointed to Latina immigrants having fewer preterm births than their education and income would predict. Princeton researchers used 2012 to 2023 US birth data for mothers from eight Latin American countries. When they measured education relative to the mother's home country, many 'low-educated' mothers turned out to be above average where they came from, and the immigrant advantage in preterm birth disappeared or reversed for most nationalities. That reframes a paradox that shows up in policy and immigration debates.
rd-2026-10-25-the-hispanic-health-parado.why_now: Online 5 days ago and not covered. Immigration and maternal health disparities are both live policy stories.
rd-2026-10-25-the-hispanic-health-parado.is_it_real: Credible reanalysis of national birth records in a major epidemiology journal. It is observational, and it refines an existing explanation (immigrants are a selected, healthier-than-average group) rather than proving there is no protective effect. Results varied by nationality, so 'the paradox is a myth' overstates it. 'Largely explained by selection on education' is the honest version. An editor will want an outside demographer's take.

studies.headline: The 'Hispanic Health Paradox' may be a statistical illusion — when education is measured correctly, immigrant mothers' birth outcome advantage largely disappears
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis

rd-2026-10-25-is-it-real-speaking-two-la.title: Is it real? Speaking two languages protects your aging brain
rd-2026-10-25-is-it-real-speaking-two-la.angle: 'Bilingual brains age better' is everywhere: language apps, brain-health listicles, doctor's-office advice. A new review of meta-analyses and prospective cohorts finds education, job complexity and mentally stimulating activities do line up with lower dementia risk, but bilingualism does not hold up the same way. The post can explain why a claim that feels obviously true failed to replicate, and what does seem to count.
rd-2026-10-25-is-it-real-speaking-two-la.why_now: Online 1 day ago, and the claim spreads on its own steadily. This is the strongest 'is it real?' receipt today.
rd-2026-10-25-is-it-real-speaking-two-la.is_it_real: This is a narrative review with no new data, not a systematic meta-analysis, so it is a receipt and an argument, not a final verdict. The underlying studies are observational. The post should cite the prospective cohorts the review relies on (to be pulled and checked from the paper) and should say 'doesn't consistently show protection', not 'proven useless'. Learning a language may still be worth doing for other reasons.

studies.headline: Speaking two languages may not actually protect the aging brain — upending a popular longevity claim
studies.caveats: observational design, narrative review (not systematic meta-analysis), no new primary data

rd-2026-10-25-kids-who-got-a-rare-platel.title: Kids who got a rare platelet disorder after their first MMR shot showed no added risk after the second
rd-2026-10-25-kids-who-got-a-rare-platel.angle: Take: a large English study of hospital and vaccination records found MMR dose 1 carries a small ITP (low-platelet) risk, about 1 in 42,900 doses. Dose 2 carried no added risk, including in 336 children who had ITP after dose 1, so doctors don't need to stop the series. It's a timely, reassuring number during measles outbreaks.
rd-2026-10-25-kids-who-got-a-rare-platel.why_now: Online 1 day ago, and measles outbreaks are in the news.
rd-2026-10-25-kids-who-got-a-rare-platel.is_it_real: Self-controlled case series on national linked records, which is the standard design for vaccine-safety signals and a strong one. The dose-2 reassurance rests on 336 children, which is solid for a rare event but not huge. Give the absolute risk, not the 2.4-fold relative figure, as the headline number.

studies.headline: Children who get a rare blood disorder after MMR dose 1 can safely receive dose 2 — large English study
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis

rd-2026-10-25-the-rsv-antibody-shot-for-.title: The RSV antibody shot for babies protects strongly at first, then fades over the first year
rd-2026-10-25-the-rsv-antibody-shot-for-.angle: Take: as RSV season starts, Queensland's first year of nirsevimab was linked to 78% fewer RSV hospitalizations in the first month of life, falling to 23% by nine months and not significant after that. That's why timing the shot to the season matters.
rd-2026-10-25-the-rsv-antibody-shot-for-.why_now: US RSV season is starting now, and parents are deciding about infant RSV protection.
rd-2026-10-25-the-rsv-antibody-shot-for-.is_it_real: Population surveillance data from one Australian state, observational, comparing against earlier birth cohorts, so changes in testing or circulation could affect the numbers. The waning curve is the useful new detail. The headline 78% applies only to month one.

studies.headline: A single RSV antibody shot cut infant hospitalizations by 78% in the first month of life
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center, short follow-up

rd-2026-10-25-small-doesn-t-mean-safe-ma.title: Small doesn't mean safe: many melanomas under 6 mm were already invasive
rd-2026-10-25-small-doesn-t-mean-safe-ma.angle: Take: the 'bigger than a pencil eraser' rule misses things. In 160 confirmed melanomas 6 mm or smaller, 42.5% were already invasive, only 30% showed three or more ABCDE warning signs, and the ABCDE score didn't predict which were invasive. Dermoscopy checks caught more of them early.
rd-2026-10-25-small-doesn-t-mean-safe-ma.why_now: Online 9 days ago, not covered. It's an easy, useful skin-check item.
rd-2026-10-25-small-doesn-t-mean-safe-ma.is_it_real: Retrospective study from Spain of lesions already confirmed as melanoma. It does NOT mean half of small moles are dangerous, which is the trap in the digest headline. It means that among small melanomas, many had already invaded. No skin-tone or sex breakdown. The item must say that in a clause.

studies.headline: Nearly Half of Tiny Melanomas — Smaller Than a Pencil Eraser — Are Already Invasive When Found
studies.caveats: observational design, retrospective, no sex-disaggregated data, single-region (Spain)

rd-2026-10-25-water-workouts-tai-chi-and.title: Water workouts, tai chi and wall sits ranked near the top for lowering blood pressure in a 284-trial analysis
rd-2026-10-25-water-workouts-tai-chi-and.angle: Take: for anyone whose knees rule out jogging, a network meta-analysis of 284 trials (18,750 adults with high or borderline blood pressure) ranked aquatic exercise first for lowering systolic pressure (about 10 mmHg), mind-body exercise first for diastolic, and isometric holds as efficient at modest weekly doses.
rd-2026-10-25-water-workouts-tai-chi-and.why_now: Online 9 days ago, not covered. It's useful and counter to the 'just walk more' default.
rd-2026-10-25-water-workouts-tai-chi-and.is_it_real: Large pool of randomized trials, but the rankings are indirect estimates across very different trials, not head-to-head tests. Mean age is 57, so frail older adults are underrepresented, and the dose figures are modeled. Say 'ranked highest in pooled trials', not 'beats the gym'.

studies.headline: Pool workouts beat the gym for lowering blood pressure, a 284-trial analysis finds
studies.caveats: Network meta-analysis pools trials that differ widely in design, supervision and participant characteristics, so head-to-head rankings are estimates rather than direct comparisons. Mean age was 56.8 years, so the oldest and frailest adults are likely underrepresented. Dose-response figures come from modelling, not from trials that directly tested those doses.

rd-2026-10-25-removing-both-ovaries-befo.title: Removing both ovaries before 45 is linked to higher type 2 diabetes risk years later
rd-2026-10-25-removing-both-ovaries-befo.angle: Evergreen explainer on surgical menopause and long-term metabolic health. In 82,472 French women followed a median of 16 years, hysterectomy plus removal of both ovaries was linked to 23% higher type 2 diabetes risk overall and about 70% higher when done before 45. Hysterectomy alone was not linked. It fits a page on what to ask before an oophorectomy and how to watch blood sugar afterward.
rd-2026-10-25-removing-both-ovaries-befo.why_now: Fresh evidence (online 2 days ago) for a topic people search for steadily. It's one cohort, so a weaker pitch than a brief.
rd-2026-10-25-removing-both-ovaries-befo.is_it_real: Large, long cohort, but observational: the women who had surgery may differ in other ways, surgical history may be self-reported, and the population is mostly White, insured French women. The 70% is a relative risk in a subgroup. The page needs absolute rates and 'linked to' language.

studies.headline: Removing ovaries before 45 is associated with a 70% higher risk of type 2 diabetes, large study finds
studies.caveats: observational design, French cohort (predominantly White, insured women — may not generalize fully to U.S. populations), self-reported surgical history possible

rd-2026-10-25-do-glp-1-weight-loss-drugs.title: Do GLP-1 weight-loss drugs cause bone loss? What the trials actually show
rd-2026-10-25-do-glp-1-weight-loss-drugs.angle: Evergreen page for women in midlife on semaglutide or tirzepatide who worry about bones. A systematic review of eight randomized trials found bone density drops in the two highest-weight-loss trials (semaglutide, liraglutide 3 mg) and no consistent effect at lower doses. No trial has measured fractures. The practical section covers a baseline DXA scan, protein and strength training.
rd-2026-10-25-do-glp-1-weight-loss-drugs.why_now: GLP-1 use among women 40 to 65 keeps rising and 'Ozempic bone loss' is a steady search. This is the latest evidence summary (online 2 days ago).
rd-2026-10-25-do-glp-1-weight-loss-drugs.is_it_real: Thin. 493 participants across eight trials, certainty rated very low for every drug, mostly people with type 2 diabetes, and bone density rather than fractures. It supports 'a signal worth asking your doctor about', not 'GLP-1s weaken bones'.

studies.headline: Do weight-loss drugs weaken bones? The evidence is thinner than the hype — but a signal is emerging
studies.caveats: Systematic review with no meta-analysis; very small total sample (n=493 across eight trials) with individual trials as small as 64 participants; certainty of evidence rated very low for every agent; most trials enrolled adults with type 2 diabetes rather than obesity alone; bone density was the outcome, not fractures; most participants were not specifically older adults.

rd-2026-10-25-ai-made-ads-beat-human-one.title: AI-made ads beat human ones on TikTok. Label them as AI and they start losing
rd-2026-10-25-ai-made-ads-beat-human-one.beat: public health, environment and tech (AI) / marketing and AI
rd-2026-10-25-ai-made-ads-beat-human-one.angle: In a Marketing Science field test with a major music label, machine-generated video ads got 26% more clicks than human-made ones on TikTok, at 98% lower cost. Five separate experiments published the same month find that telling viewers 'an AI made this' lowers how they rate the ad, the brand and their willingness to take part, and the penalty is worst on emotional, warm or cause-driven work. So performance favors AI ads, but disclosure takes some of that back. The open question for brands is which content can carry the label cheaply.
rd-2026-10-25-ai-made-ads-beat-human-one.why_now: All six papers came out online in the last 2 to 13 days, none has been covered, and brands, platforms and regulators are all moving toward AI-content labels.
rd-2026-10-25-ai-made-ads-beat-human-one.is_it_real: The lead study is the strongest marketing evidence today: four preregistered field studies with 11M+ impressions. But it was run with an industry partner that benefits from the result, it measured clicks and engagement rather than sales or streams, it covered only music promotion, and the lift showed up on TikTok but not on Meta. The disclosure studies are scenario or lab experiments that measured attitudes and intentions, not purchases. Some have small parts (one ERP study had N=27) and several abstracts don't report sample sizes. The pattern across the five is consistent. The size of the effect in live campaigns is unknown.
rd-2026-10-25-ai-made-ads-beat-human-one.other_peg: AI-content disclosure rules spreading (EU AI Act transparency obligations, platform AI labels on TikTok and Meta). Pitch agents must check the current legal status before citing any specific rule or date.

studies.headline: AI-generated video ads beat human-made ones on TikTok — at 2% of the cost
studies.caveats: Conducted with an industry partner (a major music label) whose commercial interests align with the result; limited to music-track promotion on TikTok and Meta; effects held on TikTok but not Meta; short campaign horizons; success metrics are clicks and engagement, not sales or streams.
studies.fact_check_note: ✅ Accurate: Design, four preregistered field studies, 11M+ impressions, 75 campaigns/33 tracks, 26%/10% lifts, 98% cost reduction and the Meta null all match the abstract; industry partner disclosed in Caveats.

studies.headline: People enjoy AI-made ads — until they are told an AI made them
studies.caveats: Single experiment with one set of ad stimuli; facial-coding and attitude measures rather than purchase behavior; sample size and country not specified in the abstract; immediate post-exposure measurement only.
studies.fact_check_note: ⚠️ Minor issues: Body text is faithful to the abstract; the headline slightly misstates the core result, since enjoyment was unchanged by disclosure — only the downstream evaluation changed.

studies.journal: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
studies.headline: Telling people an ad was made by AI makes it seem less creative — unless you give the AI a job title
studies.caveats: Online experiments with ad stimuli rather than observed purchases; stated attitudes and intentions; product categories and sample details limited in the abstract.
studies.fact_check_note: ⚠️ Minor issues: Core findings (three studies, attitude and purchase-intention drop via perceived creativity, product-type boundary, 'employee' framing mitigation) are accurate. The consumer story angle asserts an ethical-vs-aesthetic comparison the study did not test, and one angle relabels the mechanism as 'credibility'.

studies.headline: Disclosing AI in creative work backfires most when the content is emotional
studies.caveats: Scenario-based rather than real purchases; ERP sample of 27 is very small; participants skew young and Chinese and archival data come from one Chinese platform; the authors themselves flag generalizability limits across age, culture and creative domain.
studies.fact_check_note: ⚠️ Minor issues: Ns, methods and the legitimacy mechanism are accurate; two small over-reaches — the claim that ability was ruled out, and attributing nationality to the researchers rather than the participants.

studies.journal: Journal of Research in Interactive Marketing
studies.headline: Saying "this ad was made by AI" cuts participation in cause campaigns
studies.caveats: Experiments with recruited samples; most outcomes are intentions, though Study 1 used a consequential sharing task; two countries only; effects for AI disclosure may shift as AI-made ads become normalized.
studies.fact_check_note: ✅ Accurate: Five experiments, the consequential sharing task in Study 1, felt obligation as the supported mediator (with sincerity/authenticity not supported), Chinese and US samples, and both moderators (warmth vs competence, normative vs instrumental) are all reported correctly.

studies.journal: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
studies.headline: AI-made video ads work better when they sell with logic, not feelings — and human-like AI characters creep people out
studies.caveats: Online panel sample; forced exposure to test ads rather than natural viewing; stated attitudes, not behavior; one of the character effects did not translate into a significant difference in ad attitude.
studies.fact_check_note: ⚠️ Minor issues: Body text is precise, including the non-significant animal-character result flagged in Caveats. The headline drops the emotional/low-tech boundary condition on the uncanniness effect.

rd-2026-10-25-brands-using-ai-generated-.title: Brands using AI-generated models of color to look diverse take a credibility hit that AI white models don't
rd-2026-10-25-brands-using-ai-generated-.angle: Across five experiments, telling consumers that an ad's models were AI-generated lowered their opinion of the brand only when the synthetic models were Black, Hispanic or Asian. People read it as fake inclusion and then suspected manipulation. The penalty went away when the firm was owned by members of the community shown. That puts a number on the backlash that follows when brands use synthetic models as a cheap shortcut to diverse casting.
rd-2026-10-25-brands-using-ai-generated-.why_now: Published online 5 days ago in the Journal of Consumer Psychology with no coverage, while fashion and retail brands keep testing AI-generated models.
rd-2026-10-25-brands-using-ai-generated-.is_it_real: Five controlled experiments, probably on online panels. They measured evaluations and inferred intent, not purchases. The ownership remedy was tested only in a lab setting. The race-specific pattern is clean and well replicated within the paper, but these are US-style racial meanings and may not travel.
rd-2026-10-25-brands-using-ai-generated-.other_peg: Past brand controversies over AI-generated models (e.g. Levi's 2023 announcement that it would test AI models to add diversity). Pitch agents should confirm details and look for a current example.

studies.headline: AI-generated diversity backfires: synthetic models of color cost brands credibility
studies.caveats: Experimental studies, likely with online panels; evaluations and inferred intent rather than purchases; the ownership-signal remedy was tested in a controlled setting and racial categories and meanings are culturally specific.
studies.fact_check_note: ✅ Accurate: Matches the abstract on design (five studies), the race-asymmetric disclosure effect, the authenticity→manipulative-intent mechanism, and the ownership-signal remedy. Caveats appropriately hedge on sample details.

rd-2026-10-25-nearly-every-heart-failure.title: Nearly every heart failure drug is stopped when people with dementia enter hospice, including the diuretics that ease breathlessness, and nobody tracks what happens next
rd-2026-10-25-nearly-every-heart-failure.beat: aging, body and metabolism / end-of-life care policy
rd-2026-10-25-nearly-every-heart-failure.angle: Across 12 hospices and 1,338 patients with both heart failure and dementia, 91 to 100% of heart failure drugs were stopped at admission, including 97% of loop diuretics. Those are the drugs that relieve fluid buildup and breathlessness. Patients with dementia can't easily report those symptoms, and the data contain no record of how they fared. Some deprescribing at the end of life is sensible. Stopping the comfort drugs too, for everyone, is the question.
rd-2026-10-25-nearly-every-heart-failure.why_now: Published online 6 days ago, not covered. It fits the hospice-oversight beat already in play today (separate idea on Medicare's hospice crackdown) but is a distinct story.
rd-2026-10-25-nearly-every-heart-failure.is_it_real: A secondary observational analysis with solid numbers on discontinuation. Its central weakness is also the story: there is no data on symptoms after the drugs were stopped, so it cannot show that anyone was harmed, only that nobody measured. No age breakdown. The pitch must not say patients suffered. Before using any incentive angle (hospices pay for related drugs out of a daily rate), pitch agents should confirm with a hospice-policy expert that it applies.

studies.headline: Nearly all heart failure drugs are stopped when patients with dementia enter hospice — but no one is tracking what happens next
studies.caveats: secondary analysis, observational design, no symptom outcome data, no age breakdown reported

rd-2026-10-25-rheumatoid-arthritis-patie.title: Rheumatoid arthritis patients now reach remission twice as fast as in the 1990s, but more of them relapse
rd-2026-10-25-rheumatoid-arthritis-patie.angle: A 30-year population cohort from Olmsted County, Minnesota found one-year remission more than doubled (12.8% to 26.4%) and the median time to remission fell from 6.4 to 2.8 years. But relapse within five years of remission rose from 62.8% to 79.2%. Modern drugs got people to remission faster without making it last. That raises questions about how remission is defined and whether drugs are tapered too soon after patients get there.
rd-2026-10-25-rheumatoid-arthritis-patie.why_now: Online 2 days, not covered. The finding cuts against the usual 'biologics changed everything' story.
rd-2026-10-25-rheumatoid-arthritis-patie.is_it_real: A population-based inception cohort (1,179 people) with long follow-up that accounts for the competing risk of death. Solid for trends. It is a single, mostly white Minnesota county and observational, so it can't explain why relapse rose: changes in remission definitions, earlier and shallower remissions, or tapering could all play a part. The story needs a rheumatologist to weigh those explanations.

studies.headline: Rheumatoid arthritis patients reach remission faster than ever — but are more likely to relapse than 30 years ago
studies.caveats: single-center, observational design, geographically limited (Olmsted County, MN), competing risk of death accounted for

rd-2026-10-25-you-re-probably-not-a-bad-.title: You're probably not a 'bad returner': eight years of fashion data say returns don't lower later spending
rd-2026-10-25-you-re-probably-not-a-bad-.angle: Retailers flag, charge and sometimes ban 'serial returners.' Data on 260,698 orders from a Nordic fashion e-tailer show that nearly every long-term customer eventually returns something. Making a return had no detectable effect on how much a customer bought afterward. Spending declined just as much among matched customers who never returned anything. The cost of processing returns matters for profit; the customer's return habit didn't.
rd-2026-10-25-you-re-probably-not-a-bad-.why_now: Online 17 days and not covered, just ahead of holiday shopping and January returns season, when return fees and policies make the news.
rd-2026-10-25-you-re-probably-not-a-bad-.is_it_real: Real transaction data over 2015 to 2022 with a matched difference-in-differences design, which is better than the usual survey. But it is one retailer, one category (fashion) and one region. It is observational, so selection effects remain. The profit break-even reflects that firm's own costs. Fine to say 'one large retailer's data'; not fine to generalize to all retail.
rd-2026-10-25-you-re-probably-not-a-bad-.other_peg: Holiday returns season and retailers' mail-return fees. Pitch agents should cite current return-fee policies from named retailers.

studies.journal: The International Review of Retail Distribution and Consumer Research
studies.headline: The myth of the "bad returner": eight years of Nordic fashion data says returns don't drive future spending — or kill profit
studies.caveats: Single retailer, single category (fashion) and a single region (Nordic market); archival and observational, so matched-control DiD mitigates but does not eliminate selection effects; the profitability threshold depends on that firm's specific reverse-logistics cost structure.
studies.fact_check_note: ✅ Accurate: Sample, period, methods and the DiD statistic all match the abstract; causal language is appropriately hedged and limitations are disclosed.

rd-2026-10-25-the-30-rule-for-diversity-.title: The '30% rule' for diversity: a review of 277 studies finds a tipping point around 29%
rd-2026-10-25-the-30-rule-for-diversity-.angle: The idea behind campaigns like the 30% Club is that a group has to reach a critical mass before it changes anything. Among studies designed well enough to test that, 83% found a threshold, averaging about 29% representation. Caveat in a clause: it is a vote count of mostly correlational studies, not a pooled estimate.
rd-2026-10-25-the-30-rule-for-diversity-.why_now: A tidy number on a long-running debate about boards and teams. At 45 days old, it is too stale for a pitch.
rd-2026-10-25-the-30-rule-for-diversity-.is_it_real: An integrative review, not a meta-analysis with pooled effects. About a third of studies couldn't test the idea at all, and publication bias could inflate support. The 29% average hides wide variation. The underlying studies show links, not causes.

studies.headline: The 30% rule: how much diversity a group needs before it actually changes anything
studies.caveats: This is a conceptual review and vote-count-style synthesis of published studies, not a new meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes, so publication bias and the heavy exclusion of methodologically weak studies could inflate the apparent support. The 29% average masks wide variation across settings, outcomes and which group is underrepresented, and most underlying studies are correlational — crossing a threshold is associated with better outcomes, not proven to cause them (better-performing organizations may simply be more able to reach critical mass).
studies.fact_check_note: ⚠️ Minor issues: Core facts (277 studies, integrative conceptual review, one-third methodologically inadequate, 83% support, 29% mean threshold, SD = 6.67%) are reproduced accurately and the caveats are strong. Two small issues: the digest assigns a direction to outcomes the abstract lists neutrally, and it drops two of the four strengthening moderators (equitable contexts, stronger prior performa

rd-2026-10-25-the-liquid-death-problem-i.title: The 'Liquid Death' problem: ironic brand names make healthy products seem less healthy
rd-2026-10-25-the-liquid-death-problem-i.angle: In a set of experiments, joke or transgressive names lowered how moral a product seemed, and that dragged down how healthy it seemed. The effect held for smoothies but not milkshakes, and a clear nutrition label on the pack softened it. Caveat: lab ratings, not sales.
rd-2026-10-25-the-liquid-death-problem-i.why_now: Online 12 days, uncovered. Edgy challenger-brand names are everywhere in the drinks and snack aisle.
rd-2026-10-25-the-liquid-death-problem-i.is_it_real: Lab experiments measuring perceptions and purchase intention. The abstract gives no sample sizes or country. Edgy names did not reliably raise purchase intention either. Fictitious brands can't reproduce real brand equity.

studies.headline: The "Liquid Death" problem: joke brand names make products seem less healthy
studies.caveats: Lab-style experiments measuring perceptions and purchase intentions rather than observed sales; abstract does not report sample sizes, recruitment source or country; real-world brands like Liquid Death carry brand equity that fictitious stimuli cannot replicate.
studies.fact_check_note: ✅ Accurate: Mechanism (morality → perceived health), the virtue/vice boundary condition, the packaging-information remedy and the null on purchase intention all match the abstract; caveats correctly note missing sample details.

rd-2026-10-25-when-aldi-or-lidl-starts-c.title: When Aldi or Lidl starts carrying a big brand, rival supermarkets tend to cut its price
rd-2026-10-25-when-aldi-or-lidl-starts-c.angle: More than 300 cases in three European grocery markets show conventional supermarkets cutting prices on national brands after a discounter listed them. The listings actually raised the supermarkets' sales of those brands. Caveat: European data, and whether the cuts paid off varied by brand.
rd-2026-10-25-when-aldi-or-lidl-starts-c.why_now: Grocery prices remain a political issue, and Aldi is still expanding in the US.
rd-2026-10-25-when-aldi-or-lidl-starts-c.is_it_real: Observational market data covering short-run sales only. The fact-check flags that the digest's 'most cuts don't pay off' line leaves out the abstract's finding that cuts on average improved sales. Keep the roundup line to the price-cut pattern. The publication date has not been verified.

studies.headline: When Aldi and Lidl start stocking big brands, supermarket prices fall — but most of those cuts don't pay off
studies.caveats: Observational market data rather than a randomized experiment; three European grocery markets and leading HiLo retailers only; focuses on short-run sales effects, so longer-term brand or traffic consequences of price moves are not captured.
studies.fact_check_note: ⚠️ Minor issues: Faithful on design and on the brand/category asymmetries; drops the abstract's finding that price reductions on average further improved sales outcomes, which sits alongside the "most cuts don't pay off" result.

rd-2026-10-25-exercise-alcohol-medicatio.title: Exercise, alcohol, medications and even your period can make an allergic reaction more severe
rd-2026-10-25-exercise-alcohol-medicatio.angle: Nearly 17,000 cases in the European Anaphylaxis Registry: medication was the most common cofactor in adults (41%), then exercise (27%). Menstruation was suspected in 4% of adult cases. More cofactors at once went with worse reactions and a later start of symptoms after eating a trigger food. Caveat: cofactors were suspected, not proven.
rd-2026-10-25-exercise-alcohol-medicatio.why_now: Online 2 days, uncovered, with a useful takeaway for anyone carrying an epinephrine auto-injector.
rd-2026-10-25-exercise-alcohol-medicatio.is_it_real: A large registry, but it is observational and cofactors were judged by suspicion. It describes how often cofactors appear, not how much each raises risk. European population.

studies.headline: Menstruation, Exercise, and Alcohol Can Make Allergic Reactions More Dangerous — Here's What the Data Show
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, European registry population (may not generalize globally), cofactor data based on suspicion rather than confirmed causation

rd-2026-10-25-in-later-life-mood-matters.title: In later life, mood matters as much as blood pressure: two quarter-million-person studies link low mood combos to dementia and disability
rd-2026-10-25-in-later-life-mood-matters.angle: In about 247,000 Dutch adults, the late-life group combining loneliness, depression and inactivity had the highest dementia risk of any risk-factor group (hazard ratio 1.23). In about 258,000 adults across six international aging studies, low mood plus poor word recall was linked to roughly double the risk of needing help with daily tasks (RR 2.19). Caveat: both observational, effects modest.
rd-2026-10-25-in-later-life-mood-matters.why_now: Both online within 3 days, both uncovered. Paired, they make one useful item.
rd-2026-10-25-in-later-life-mood-matters.is_it_real: Very large cohorts, but observational with self-reported risk factors. The dementia hazard ratios are modest. Cognition was measured with one word-recall task. They show links, not causes. Say 'linked to.'

studies.headline: Loneliness plus inactivity beat out blood pressure and diabetes as the riskiest dementia combination in a quarter-million adults
studies.caveats: Observational cohort — cannot establish that these clusters cause dementia; risk factors were largely self-reported in a single survey wave; Dutch population may not generalize elsewhere; hazard ratios are modest in size.

studies.headline: Low mood plus a slipping memory: the combination that doubles the risk of losing independence
studies.caveats: Observational pooled cohort data — it cannot show that depression or memory decline causes disability; depressive symptoms were self-reported and cognition was measured with a single word-recall task; mortality hazards were nonproportional; the harmonized cohorts differ in measurement and culture, so findings may not translate evenly to every population.

rd-2026-10-25-lecanemab-outside-trials-b.title: Lecanemab outside trials: brain-swelling risk is about one in three for people with two APOE4 copies
rd-2026-10-25-lecanemab-outside-trials-b.angle: Pooled data from 37 real-world studies: about 15% of patients overall had brain swelling or small bleeds (ARIA). The rate was 34% with two APOE4 copies versus 11% with none, and 23% versus 11.5% with or without existing microbleeds. US rates ran about double Asian rates. Caveat: there were no control groups, so these studies can't show cognitive benefit.
rd-2026-10-25-lecanemab-outside-trials-b.why_now: Online 4 days, uncovered. Families weighing infusions can get both answers (genotype and MRI) before the first dose.
rd-2026-10-25-lecanemab-outside-trials-b.is_it_real: A meta-analysis of uncontrolled observational cohorts with substantial heterogeneity and follow-up of 12 months or less. The risk numbers are useful and broadly match the trials. Nothing here speaks to whether the drug works.

studies.headline: Lecanemab in the real world: brain swelling and bleeding risk hinges on genes and pre-existing microbleeds
studies.caveats: Meta-analysis of observational real-world cohorts with no control arms, so cognitive outcomes cannot be interpreted as efficacy; substantial heterogeneity between regions; overlapping patient cohorts across included studies required statistical adjustment; follow-up largely 12 months or less.

rd-2026-10-25-the-first-vaccine-for-crim.title: The first vaccine for Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a tick-borne virus, passed its first human safety test
rd-2026-10-25-the-first-vaccine-for-crim.angle: An Oxford-style adenovirus-vector vaccine against a WHO priority virus that kills up to 40% of people it infects was well tolerated in 46 UK adults and produced antibodies after two doses. Caveat: phase 1 safety only, years from use.
rd-2026-10-25-the-first-vaccine-for-crim.why_now: Online 2 days in Lancet Infectious Diseases and not covered. It is a first-in-human milestone.
rd-2026-10-25-the-first-vaccine-for-crim.is_it_real: Phase 1: small, open-label, not randomized, single center, short follow-up. It shows safety and an immune response, not protection. Too early for a pitch unless a climate-and-ticks story gives it a stake.

studies.headline: First human trial of a Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever vaccine shows it's safe and triggers immune response
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), open-label, non-randomised, single-center, short follow-up
